newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac defies Israel over Orient House PLO visit.
newsitem.headline: Chirac defies Israel over Orient House PLO visit.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac sparked a diplomatic clash with Israel on Thursday over a disputed Palestinian headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem, two days before he begins a sensitive Middle East tour.

Chirac's spokeswoman said Foreign Minister Herve de Charette would not accompany the president to Israel next week as planned and that in his place a junior French minister would visit Orient House, the unofficial PLO headquarters in the city.

She also said Chirac would reaffirm France's call for a Palestinian state in his speeches in Israel and the Palestinian territories and stress that a lasting settlement could only be based on an exchange of land for peace.

Spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said Chirac had informed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September of his wish to send de Charette to Orient House in line with European Union policy on maintaining the status quo in Jerusalem.
Netanyahu had objected, and prolonged negotiations between the two sides had not changed the Israeli stance, she said.

"The president has decided with great regret that Mr de Charette will not accompany him to Israel, although he will be on all the other stages of the trip," Colonna said. "The president has decided that junior health minister Herve Gaymard will be charged with going to Orient House."
It was not certain the Israeli authorities would let Gaymard visit the PLO office. The Israeli Embassy declined comment.
However Colonna said Chirac did not seek a confrontation and she believed this solution was "agreeable to the Israelis".

Israel, which claims sovereignty over the whole of Greater Jerusalem, argues that President Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority is in breach of peace agreements by conducting business from Orient House.

EU policy is that foreign ministers should visit the office, headed by Palestinian minister Faisal al-Husseini, on each official visit to uphold the status quo in the city pending final status negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians.
The diplomatic clash flared two days before Chirac begins a tour of Syria, Israel, the Palestinian territories, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt.

Colonna said that at each stop on his six-day journey, the president would stress four basic principes: land for peace, the right of all states in the region to exercise full sovereignty over their entire territory, the Palestinians' right to "free self-determination, that is to say to the foundation of a state" and the right of all states, including Israel, to security.
Chirac would convey the European Union's message that the Middle East must not sacrifice the opportunity for peace born of the 1993 Israel-PLO accords.

While it was up to the parties to negotiate detailed peace accords, the European Union could and should play a helpful role since it was the main financial sponsor of the peace process and a Mediterranean neighbour of the region.
